lessons.correct: The low-level control language for machines, which AI can generate

lessons.title: Feedback from the Physical World
lessons.content: A key challenge is incorporating feedback. If a robot fails to grasp an object, this physical feedback (e.g., from a force sensor) must be translated back into the AI's context so it can retry.

lessons.question: Why is feedback important when prompting for physical systems?
options: It allows the AI to learn from physical failures and successes
Physical feedback is not important
The AI only needs text feedback
lessons.correct: It allows the AI to learn from physical failures and successes

lessons.title: Safety Constraints are Paramount
lessons.content: Prompts for physical systems must have extremely strong safety constraints to prevent the AI from generating commands that could damage the equipment or cause harm to humans.

lessons.question: What is the most critical aspect of prompting for robotics?
options: Speed of operation
Safety constraints to prevent physical harm
The robot's color
lessons.correct: Safety constraints to prevent physical harm

lessons.title: Simulation-to-Reality Transfer
lessons.content: Often, prompts are first tested in a physics-based simulation. The goal is to develop prompts that work in simulation and can then be transferred to the real-world robot with minimal changes.

lessons.question: What is 'simulation-to-reality transfer'?
options: Testing prompts in a virtual environment before deploying on a real robot
Building a simulation of a real robot after it has been deployed
Keeping all work purely in simulation
lessons.correct: Testing prompts in a virtual environment before deploying on a real robot

lessons.question: What is an 'affordance' in robotics prompting?
options: The cost of the robot
The actions a robot can perform on an object (e.g., a mug can be 'grasped')
How much a user can afford to pay
lessons.correct: The actions a robot can perform on an object (e.g., a mug can be 'grasped')

lessons.title: Prompting for Affordances
lessons.content: A prompt can ask an AI to look at an object (via a camera) and determine its 'affordances'—the possible actions that can be performed on it (e.g., a door can be 'pushed' or 'pulled').

modules.title: Prompting for Large-Scale AI Orchestration

lessons.title: Beyond a Single Agent
lessons.content: AI orchestration involves using prompts to manage and coordinate a fleet or swarm of multiple AI agents working together on a complex task.

lessons.question: What is AI orchestration?
options: Using only one powerful AI agent
Managing and coordinating multiple AI agents
Playing music with AI
lessons.correct: Managing and coordinating multiple AI agents

lessons.title: The 'Orchestrator' Prompt
lessons.content: A central 'orchestrator' or 'manager' agent is given a high-level prompt that instructs it to decompose a task and delegate sub-tasks to specialized 'worker' agents.

lessons.question: What is the role of an 'orchestrator' agent?
options: To perform all the work itself
To decompose a task and delegate it to worker agents
To monitor the weather
lessons.correct: To decompose a task and delegate it to worker agents

lessons.title: Role-Based Agent Prompting
lessons.content: Each worker agent is initialized with a specific role-based prompt, e.g., 'You are a data analyst agent,' 'You are a content writer agent,' 'You are a code reviewer agent.'

lessons.question: How are worker agents typically specialized?
options: Through specific, role-based prompts
They are all given the same generic prompt
They choose their own roles randomly
lessons.correct: Through specific, role-based prompts

lessons.title: Communication Protocols
lessons.content: The orchestration prompt must define a communication protocol, specifying the format (e.g., JSON) in which agents should pass information and results to each other.

lessons.question: Why is a communication protocol important for multi-agent systems?
options: To ensure agents can share information in a structured way
To prevent agents from communicating
Agents do not need to communicate
lessons.correct: To ensure agents can share information in a structured way

lessons.title: Hierarchical Task Structures
lessons.content: Orchestration can be hierarchical. A top-level manager agent can delegate to mid-level managers, who in turn delegate to workers, mirroring a corporate structure.

lessons.question: What does a hierarchical orchestration structure resemble?
options: A flat, single-layer network
A corporate management structure
A circle
lessons.correct: A corporate management structure

lessons.title: Resource Allocation Prompts
lessons.content: The orchestrator can be prompted to allocate resources, such as assigning more computationally expensive models or tools to agents working on more critical sub-tasks.

lessons.question: What is 'resource allocation' in AI orchestration?
options: Giving all agents the exact same resources
Assigning resources (e.g., powerful models) based on task priority
Taking away all resources from agents
lessons.correct: Assigning resources (e.g., powerful models) based on task priority

lessons.title: Consensus and Voting Mechanisms
lessons.content: For critical decisions, the orchestrator can prompt multiple agents to perform the same task and then use a voting or consensus mechanism to determine the most reliable result.

lessons.question: How can an orchestrator improve the reliability of a result?
options: By using a consensus mechanism from multiple agent outputs
By trusting the first agent that responds
By randomly picking one agent's answer
lessons.correct: By using a consensus mechanism from multiple agent outputs

lessons.title: Conflict Resolution Prompts
lessons.content: When agents produce conflicting results, the orchestrator can be prompted to initiate a 'debate' or a mediation process to resolve the discrepancy.

lessons.question: What happens when agents produce conflicting results?
options: The system crashes
The orchestrator can use a prompt to initiate a resolution process
The first result is always chosen
lessons.correct: The orchestrator can use a prompt to initiate a resolution process

lessons.title: Scalability and Load Balancing
lessons.content: The orchestration system must be designed to be scalable, with prompts that allow it to spin up or shut down worker agents based on the current workload (load balancing).

lessons.question: What does load balancing achieve in a multi-agent system?
options: It distributes the workload efficiently across agents
It gives all the work to one agent
It stops all agents from working
lessons.correct: It distributes the workload efficiently across agents

lessons.question: What is a major challenge in large-scale AI orchestration?
options: Ensuring all agents remain aligned with the overall goal
Making sure the agents use a lot of tokens
It is a simple and solved problem
lessons.correct: Ensuring all agents remain aligned with the overall goal

lessons.title: Goal Alignment and Drift
lessons.content: A major challenge is ensuring that all agents, especially in long, complex tasks, remain aligned with the orchestrator's primary goal and do not 'drift' into irrelevant or counter-productive work.

modules.title: Hybrid AI: Combining Symbolic AI with LLMs via Prompts

lessons.title: The Two Schools of AI
lessons.content: Hybrid AI seeks to combine the strengths of Large Language Models (statistical, generative) with Symbolic AI (logical, rule-based) to create more robust and trustworthy systems.

lessons.question: What is the goal of Hybrid AI?
options: To prove that LLMs are superior to all other AI
To combine the strengths of LLMs and Symbolic AI
To only use Symbolic AI
lessons.correct: To combine the strengths of LLMs and Symbolic AI

lessons.title: LLM as a 'Natural Language Interface'
lessons.content: In this pattern, the LLM's role is to translate a user's natural language query into a formal, structured query that a Symbolic AI system (like a rule engine or knowledge graph) can understand.

lessons.question: What is a common role for an LLM in a hybrid system?
options: To act as a natural language interface to a symbolic system
To perform all the logical reasoning itself
To generate random images
lessons.correct: To act as a natural language interface to a symbolic system

lessons.title: Symbolic System as a 'Fact-Checker'
lessons.content: An LLM can be prompted to generate a draft answer, which is then passed to a symbolic system (e.g., a database, knowledge graph) for fact-checking and validation before being shown to the user.

lessons.question: How can a symbolic system be used to improve an LLM's output?
options: By acting as a fact-checker to validate the LLM's claims
By adding creative, fictional details to the output
It cannot improve the output
lessons.correct: By acting as a fact-checker to validate the LLM's claims

lessons.title: Prompting for Knowledge Graph Queries
lessons.content: A prompt can instruct an LLM to convert a question like 'Who are the actors in the movies directed by Christopher Nolan?' into a formal query language like SPARQL for a knowledge graph.

lessons.question: What can an LLM be prompted to generate for a knowledge graph?
options: A natural language summary
A formal query in a language like SPARQL
A new password
lessons.correct: A formal query in a language like SPARQL

lessons.title: Rule-Based Constraint Checking
lessons.content: An LLM can generate a plan or a configuration, and a rule-based engine can check if it violates any hard constraints (e.g., 'A manager cannot approve their own expense report').

lessons.question: What is the role of a rule engine in a hybrid system?
options: To check if an LLM's output violates any hard-coded rules
To generate creative text
To agree with everything the LLM says
lessons.correct: To check if an LLM's output violates any hard-coded rules

lessons.title: Combining with Mathematical Solvers
lessons.content: For quantitative problems, an LLM can be prompted to identify the variables and equations from a word problem and then pass them to a dedicated mathematical solver for a precise calculation.

lessons.question: Why would you combine an LLM with a mathematical solver?
options: Because LLMs are perfect at math
To have the LLM extract the problem setup and the solver perform the precise calculation
To make the problem harder to solve
lessons.correct: To have the LLM extract the problem setup and the solver perform the precise calculation

lessons.title: LLM for Explanation Generation
lessons.content: After a symbolic system produces a result (e.g., a complex logical deduction), an LLM can be prompted to translate that formal result into an easy-to-understand, natural language explanation.

lessons.question: How can an LLM help with the output of a symbolic system?
options: By translating a formal, logical output into a natural language explanation
By checking the symbolic system's logic
By hiding the output
lessons.correct: By translating a formal, logical output into a natural language explanation

lessons.title: Neuro-Symbolic Programming
lessons.content: This involves creating programs where LLMs (neuro) can call functions from a traditional, symbolic codebase and vice-versa, with prompts acting as the interface layer.

lessons.question: What does neuro-symbolic programming involve?
options: Using only neural networks
Creating programs where LLMs and symbolic code can call each other
Using only symbolic code
lessons.correct: Creating programs where LLMs and symbolic code can call each other

lessons.title: Improving Trust and Explainability
lessons.content: A key benefit of hybrid systems is that the symbolic components provide a level of rigor, determinism, and explainability that purely generative models often lack.

lessons.question: What is a major benefit of using a hybrid AI approach?
options: It increases the trust and explainability of the system
It makes the system fully generative and unpredictable
It is always the cheapest option
lessons.correct: It increases the trust and explainability of the system

lessons.question: In a hybrid system, which component is better for handling ambiguity?
options: The symbolic component
The LLM component
Both are equally good
lessons.correct: The LLM component

lessons.title: Handling Ambiguity and Creativity
lessons.content: The LLM component excels at handling ambiguous, fuzzy, or creative tasks, while the symbolic component excels at tasks requiring precision and logical consistency.

modules.title: Prompt Engineering for Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) APIs

lessons.title: Prompting as API Interaction
lessons.content: When using a commercial AI model (MaaS), the prompt is the primary way to interact with the API. Designing robust, efficient, and secure prompts is key to building a successful application.

lessons.question: In a MaaS context, what is the prompt equivalent to?
options: The user interface
The core method of interacting with the API
A database
lessons.correct: The core method of interacting with the API

lessons.title: System vs. User Prompts
lessons.content: MaaS APIs often distinguish between a 'system' prompt (which sets the AI's persona and high-level rules) and 'user' prompts (the ongoing turns in a conversation).

lessons.question: What is the typical function of a 'system' prompt in a MaaS API?
options: To ask a specific question in a conversation
To set the AI's overall persona and rules
To end the conversation
lessons.correct: To set the AI's overall persona and rules

lessons.title: Controlling API Parameters
lessons.content: Besides the prompt text, you control the AI's behavior through API parameters like 'temperature' (randomness), 'max_tokens' (length), and 'stop_sequences' (when to end).

lessons.question: What does the 'temperature' parameter in an AI API typically control?
options: The factual accuracy of the output
The randomness or creativity of the output
The physical temperature of the server
lessons.correct: The randomness or creativity of the output

lessons.title: Structured Output with JSON Mode
lessons.content: Many APIs offer a 'JSON mode,' which, when prompted correctly, constrains the model to only output valid, parsable JSON. This is crucial for predictable application logic.

lessons.question: What is the benefit of using 'JSON mode' in an API?
options: It constrains the output to be valid JSON, making it easy to parse
It allows the AI to output free-form, creative text
It makes the output a random string
lessons.correct: It constrains the output to be valid JSON, making it easy to parse

lessons.title: Function Calling and Tool Use
lessons.content: Modern APIs allow you to define 'tools' (functions) in your code. You can prompt the AI to generate the JSON arguments to call one of these tools, enabling it to interact with external systems.

lessons.question: What does the 'function calling' feature of an API allow an AI to do?
options: To generate the arguments needed to call a function in your application's code
To call functions on its own server
To ignore all functions
lessons.correct: To generate the arguments needed to call a function in your application's code

lessons.title: API Cost Management
lessons.content: Every API call costs money. Prompts should be engineered for efficiency, and application logic should include budget controls, caching, and smart model selection to manage costs.

lessons.question: What is a key consideration when building an application on a MaaS API?
options: Using as many tokens as possible
Managing the monetary cost of API calls
Ignoring the API's performance
lessons.correct: Managing the monetary cost of API calls

lessons.title: Rate Limiting and Retries
lessons.content: Production applications must handle API rate limits. Your code should implement exponential backoff and retry logic when a prompt request fails due to rate limiting.

lessons.question: What should your application do when it hits an API rate limit?
options: Crash immediately
Implement a retry mechanism with exponential backoff
Send requests even faster
lessons.correct: Implement a retry mechanism with exponential backoff

lessons.title: Versioning Prompts and Models
lessons.content: AI models are constantly updated. It's crucial to version your prompts and lock your application to a specific model version to prevent unexpected behavior changes when a new model is released.

lessons.question: Why should you lock your application to a specific model version?
options: To prevent unexpected behavior changes when the model is updated
To always have the latest, untested model
Model versions never change
lessons.correct: To prevent unexpected behavior changes when the model is updated

lessons.title: Security and API Key Management
lessons.content: Never expose your API keys in client-side code. All API calls should be routed through a secure backend server that manages the keys.

lessons.question: Where should your MaaS API key be stored and used?
options: In the client-side JavaScript code
In a secure backend server
In a public GitHub repository
lessons.correct: In a secure backend server

lessons.question: What is a 'prompt template' in the context of API development?
options: A reusable prompt structure with placeholders for dynamic data
A single, hard-coded prompt
A feature of the AI model itself
lessons.correct: A reusable prompt structure with placeholders for dynamic data

lessons.title: Using Prompt Templates
lessons.content: Instead of hard-coding prompts, use prompt templates (e.g., f-strings in Python) that have placeholders for dynamic data. This makes prompts more maintainable, reusable, and secure.

modules.title: Temporal Prompting: Reasoning about Time and Events

lessons.title: The Challenge of Time
lessons.content: LLMs do not inherently understand the passage of time or causality. Temporal prompting involves structuring prompts to help an AI reason about timelines, sequences, and cause-and-effect.

lessons.question: What is a fundamental challenge for LLMs regarding time?
options: They have a perfect, innate understanding of time
They do not inherently understand time or causality
They can predict the future with 100% accuracy
lessons.correct: They do not inherently understand time or causality

lessons.title: Using Timestamps and Structured Data
lessons.content: When providing context, use clear, standardized timestamps (like ISO 8601) and structure events in a chronological format (e.g., a list of JSON objects with a 'timestamp' key).

lessons.question: How can you help an AI understand a sequence of events?
options: By describing the events in a random order
By using standardized timestamps and a chronological structure
By avoiding any mention of dates or times
lessons.correct: By using standardized timestamps and a chronological structure

lessons.title: Prompting for Timelines
lessons.content: You can prompt an AI to take a block of unstructured text and generate a structured timeline of events, extracting the key actions and their corresponding times.

lessons.question: What is a common temporal task for an AI?
options: To generate a structured timeline from unstructured text
To create a fictional story about time travel
To ignore all time-related information
lessons.correct: To generate a structured timeline from unstructured text

lessons.title: Causal Reasoning Prompts
lessons.content: To reason about causality, a prompt might ask, 'Given event A happened at T1 and event B happened at T2, what is the most likely causal relationship between them?'

lessons.question: How can you prompt for causal reasoning?
options: By asking the AI to determine the likely cause-and-effect relationship between events
By assuming all events are unrelated
By asking the AI for its favorite color
lessons.correct: By asking the AI to determine the likely cause-and-effect relationship between events

lessons.title: Forecasting and Prediction
lessons.content: For forecasting, a prompt must provide historical time-series data and ask the AI to 'extrapolate the trend' or 'predict the value for the next quarter based on the provided data.'

lessons.question: What is required in a prompt for AI-based forecasting?
options: Historical time-series data and a clear prediction task
No data is required
Only the most recent data point
lessons.correct: Historical time-series data and a clear prediction task

lessons.title: The Knowledge Cutoff Problem
lessons.content: Foundation models have a 'knowledge cutoff' date; they are not aware of events that happened after their training. Prompts must be designed with this limitation in mind, often using RAG to provide up-to-date information.

lessons.question: What is the 'knowledge cutoff' date?
options: The date after which the AI's training data does not include new events
The date the AI was first created
The AI has no knowledge cutoff
lessons.correct: The date after which the AI's training data does not include new events

lessons.title: Reasoning about Relative Time
lessons.content: Prompts can test understanding of relative time with phrases like 'three days before the event' or 'two hours after the initial report.'

lessons.question: What is 'relative time' in a prompt?
options: A specific date and time like '2023-10-27T10:00:00Z'
A time described in relation to another event, like 'one day later'
A time that is not real
lessons.correct: A time described in relation to another event, like 'one day later'

lessons.title: State Change Tracking
lessons.content: For processes that evolve over time, the prompt can ask the AI to track the state of an entity at different points in time (e.g., 'What was the project status on Monday vs. Friday?').

lessons.question: What is 'state change tracking'?
options: Keeping the state of an entity the same
Tracking how an entity changes over a period of time
Ignoring the state of an entity
lessons.correct: Tracking how an entity changes over a period of time

lessons.title: Counterfactual Time Prompts
lessons.content: A sophisticated prompt can ask for counterfactual reasoning about time, e.g., 'If event A had not happened at T1, what would have been the likely outcome at T3?'

lessons.question: What does a counterfactual time prompt ask?
options: To describe what actually happened
To reason about what would have happened if a past event were different
To predict the future with certainty
lessons.correct: To reason about what would have happened if a past event were different

lessons.question: Why is it important to be precise with temporal language in prompts?
options: Vague terms like 'recently' can be easily misinterpreted by the AI
It makes the prompt shorter
The AI understands all temporal terms perfectly
lessons.correct: Vague terms like 'recently' can be easily misinterpreted by the AI

lessons.title: Avoiding Ambiguous Language
lessons.content: Avoid vague temporal terms like 'recently' or 'a while ago.' Instead, provide concrete dates, times, or a clear sequence of events to prevent misinterpretation.

modules.title: Psychology of Prompting: Influencing AI Behavior and Persona

lessons.title: Prompting as a Psychological Act
lessons.content: Prompting is not just a technical instruction; it's a psychological one. The way a prompt is phrased can influence the AI's persona, tone, and even its apparent 'emotional state.'

lessons.question: How can prompting be viewed from a psychological perspective?
options: As a way to influence the AI's persona and tone
As a purely technical and logical process
It has no psychological dimension
lessons.correct: As a way to influence the AI's persona and tone

lessons.title: The Power of Persona
lessons.content: Assigning a detailed persona in the system prompt (e.g., 'You are a witty, skeptical expert') is one of the most powerful ways to shape the style and content of all subsequent outputs.

lessons.question: What is the effect of assigning a detailed persona to an AI?
options: It has little to no effect on the output
It powerfully shapes the style and content of the output
It makes the AI refuse to answer
lessons.correct: It powerfully shapes the style and content of the output

lessons.title: Emotional Contagion
lessons.content: The emotional tone of the user's prompt can influence the AI's response. A polite and positive prompt is more likely to elicit a helpful and positive response, and vice-versa.

lessons.question: What is 'emotional contagion' in prompting?
options: The AI always responds with a neutral tone
The emotional tone of the prompt can influence the tone of the AI's response
The AI catches computer viruses
lessons.correct: The emotional tone of the prompt can influence the tone of the AI's response

lessons.title: Using Cognitive Biases
lessons.content: Prompts can leverage cognitive biases. For example, the 'framing effect' can be used by asking the AI to 'highlight the benefits' versus 'list the risks' of a topic.

lessons.question: What is an example of using the 'framing effect' in a prompt?
options: Asking a completely neutral question
Asking the AI to focus on either the positive or negative aspects of a topic
Asking the AI to frame a picture
lessons.correct: Asking the AI to focus on either the positive or negative aspects of a topic

lessons.title: The 'Tip' Technique
lessons.content: Some research suggests that adding a phrase like 'I will tip you $200 for a perfect answer' can psychologically motivate the model to produce a more thorough and higher-quality response.

lessons.question: What is the 'tip' technique in prompting?
options: Actually sending money to the AI company
Adding a phrase about a hypothetical reward to motivate a better response
Asking the AI for a stock tip
lessons.correct: Adding a phrase about a hypothetical reward to motivate a better response

lessons.title: Reducing Sycophancy
lessons.content: AI models can be 'sycophantic,' tending to agree with the user's stated opinion. To counter this, prompt the AI to 'play devil's advocate' or 'provide counterarguments.'

lessons.question: How can you prompt an AI to be less sycophantic?
options: By asking it to agree with you
By asking it to play devil's advocate or provide counterarguments
Sycophancy cannot be reduced
lessons.correct: By asking it to play devil's advocate or provide counterarguments

lessons.title: Vulnerability and Honesty
lessons.content: Phrasing a prompt in a way that shows vulnerability or admits a lack of knowledge (e.g., 'I'm a complete beginner, please explain this simply') can elicit a more patient and empathetic response from the AI.

lessons.question: What effect can admitting vulnerability in a prompt have?
options: It can elicit a more patient and simple explanation
It will cause the AI to give a more complex answer
It has no effect
lessons.correct: It can elicit a more patient and simple explanation

lessons.title: Setting Expectations of Effort
lessons.content: Starting a prompt with a phrase like 'This is very important for my career' can signal to the model that a high-effort, detailed response is required.

lessons.question: How can you signal to an AI that a high-effort response is needed?
options: By starting the prompt with a statement about the task's importance
By keeping the prompt as short as possible
By telling the AI the task is not important
lessons.correct: By starting the prompt with a statement about the task's importance

lessons.title: The 'Take a Deep Breath' Technique
lessons.content: For complex reasoning tasks, starting the prompt with a calming, focusing phrase like 'Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step' has been shown to improve performance.

lessons.question: What is the 'take a deep breath' technique used for?
options: To improve the AI's performance on complex reasoning tasks
To make the AI respond faster
To get a less detailed answer
lessons.correct: To improve the AI's performance on complex reasoning tasks

lessons.question: What is an ethical concern with using psychological prompts?
options: They could be used to create manipulative or deceptive AI behaviors
They make the AI less effective
There are no ethical concerns
lessons.correct: They could be used to create manipulative or deceptive AI behaviors

lessons.title: Ethical Implications
lessons.content: The power to psychologically influence AI behavior carries significant ethical weight. These techniques must be used responsibly to create helpful and transparent systems, not manipulative ones.

modules.title: Advanced RAG: HyDE, Self-Correction, and Knowledge Graphs

lessons.title: Limitations of Basic RAG
lessons.content: Basic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can struggle if the user's query is poorly phrased or if the retrieved documents contain conflicting or irrelevant information.

lessons.question: What is a limitation of basic RAG?
options: It works perfectly with any query
It can fail if the query is poor or documents are irrelevant
It does not retrieve documents
lessons.correct: It can fail if the query is poor or documents are irrelevant

lessons.title: HyDE: Hypothetical Document Embeddings
lessons.content: HyDE is a technique where the AI first generates a hypothetical, ideal answer to the user's query. It then uses the embedding of this *hypothetical* answer to find real documents that are semantically similar.

lessons.question: What does the HyDE technique use to search for documents?
options: The user's original query
A hypothetical answer generated by the AI
A random string
lessons.correct: A hypothetical answer generated by the AI

lessons.title: Self-Correcting RAG (Self-RAG)
lessons.content: In Self-RAG, the AI retrieves documents and then critiques them, deciding if they are relevant. If not, it re-queries with a refined search term. It also critiques its own final answer for factuality based on the sources.

lessons.question: What is a key feature of Self-RAG?
options: It critiques the retrieved documents and its own final answer
It accepts the first document it finds
It never generates a final answer
lessons.correct: It critiques the retrieved documents and its own final answer

lessons.title: RAG with Knowledge Graphs
lessons.content: Instead of retrieving unstructured text chunks, this approach has the AI query a structured knowledge graph. This provides more precise, factual data and allows for reasoning about relationships between entities.

lessons.question: What is an advantage of using a knowledge graph for RAG?
options: It provides more structured and precise factual data
It provides unstructured text paragraphs
It is easier to set up than a vector database
lessons.correct: It provides more structured and precise factual data

lessons.title: Query Transformation
lessons.content: This involves using an LLM to take a conversational user query and transform it into several more precise, keyword-based sub-queries to improve the chances of finding relevant documents.

lessons.question: What is the goal of query transformation in RAG?
options: To make the user's query more vague
To transform a conversational query into more precise sub-queries
To use the user's query exactly as it is
lessons.correct: To transform a conversational query into more precise sub-queries

lessons.title: Document Re-ranking
lessons.content: After an initial retrieval, a second, more sophisticated (but slower) model can be used to re-rank the top N documents for relevance to the query before they are passed to the final generation step.

lessons.question: What is the purpose of a re-ranking step in a RAG pipeline?
options: To re-order the retrieved documents for better relevance
To randomly shuffle the documents
To retrieve more documents
lessons.correct: To re-order the retrieved documents for better relevance

lessons.title: Hybrid Search
lessons.content: Hybrid search combines traditional keyword-based search (like BM25) with modern semantic (vector) search. This ensures that documents with exact keyword matches are not missed, even if their semantics are slightly different.

lessons.question: What two types of search are combined in 'hybrid search'?
options: Keyword-based search and semantic search
Image search and audio search
Random search and direct search
lessons.correct: Keyword-based search and semantic search

lessons.title: Multi-Hop RAG
lessons.content: For complex questions, multi-hop RAG allows the AI to perform a series of retrievals. The answer from the first retrieval is used to formulate the query for the second retrieval, and so on.

lessons.question: When is multi-hop RAG useful?
options: For simple questions that require one fact
For complex questions that require chaining multiple pieces of information
It is never useful
lessons.correct: For complex questions that require chaining multiple pieces of information

lessons.title: Contextual Compression
lessons.content: Instead of passing whole documents into the final prompt, contextual compression extracts only the most relevant sentences from each document, reducing noise and cost.

lessons.question: What is 'contextual compression' in RAG?
options: Passing full documents to the LLM
Extracting only the most relevant sentences from documents
Making the documents larger
lessons.correct: Extracting only the most relevant sentences from documents

lessons.question: What is 'routing' in an advanced RAG system?
options: Sending every query to the same database
Using an LLM to decide which data source (e.g., knowledge graph, vector DB) is best for a given query
Sending the query to a random place
lessons.correct: Using an LLM to decide which data source (e.g., knowledge graph, vector DB) is best for a given query

lessons.title: Query Routing
lessons.content: In a system with multiple data sources (e.g., a vector database for text, a knowledge graph for facts), a 'router' LLM can first analyze the query and decide which data source is the most appropriate one to search.

modules.title: Compression Techniques for Prompts and Context

lessons.title: The Need for Compression
lessons.content: Prompt and context compression techniques aim to reduce the number of tokens sent to an LLM without losing critical information, in order to save costs and reduce latency.

lessons.question: What are the two main goals of prompt compression?
options: To increase cost and latency
To save costs and reduce latency
To make prompts longer
lessons.correct: To save costs and reduce latency

lessons.title: Instruction Abbreviation
lessons.content: This simple technique involves finding shorter synonyms and removing verbose, polite, or unnecessary phrasing from the instructional part of the prompt.

lessons.question: What is instruction abbreviation?
options: Making instructions as long as possible
Using shorter synonyms and removing verbose phrasing
Adding unnecessary details
lessons.correct: Using shorter synonyms and removing verbose phrasing

lessons.title: LLM-Based Context Summarization
lessons.content: Before sending a large document as context, use a faster, cheaper LLM to generate a concise summary of it. The summary is then used as the context for the more expensive LLM.

lessons.question: How can one LLM be used to compress context for another?
options: By using a cheap LLM to summarize a document for an expensive LLM
This is not a valid technique
By having the LLM expand the document
lessons.correct: By using a cheap LLM to summarize a document for an expensive LLM

lessons.title: Selective Context
lessons.content: Instead of full-text RAG, use a model to extract only the most relevant facts or sentences from retrieved documents to build a minimal, targeted context.

lessons.question: What is the 'selective context' technique?
options: Using the entire retrieved document as context
Extracting only the most relevant sentences to use as context
Using a random part of the document
lessons.correct: Extracting only the most relevant sentences to use as context

lessons.title: Abstractive vs. Extractive Summarization
lessons.content: Extractive summarization pulls key sentences, while abstractive summarization generates new, more concise sentences. Abstractive is often shorter but risks losing fidelity.

lessons.question: What is the main difference between abstractive and extractive summarization?
options: Extractive pulls existing sentences; abstractive generates new ones
They are the same thing
Extractive is always better
lessons.correct: Extractive pulls existing sentences; abstractive generates new ones

lessons.title: Token-Level Compression (Token Dropping)
lessons.content: This automated technique identifies and removes tokens from the context that are predicted to have the least impact on the final answer, such as stop words or redundant adjectives.

lessons.question: What is token dropping?
options: Adding more tokens to the context
Removing tokens that are predicted to be least important
Randomly removing tokens
lessons.correct: Removing tokens that are predicted to be least important

lessons.title: Conversation History Pruning
lessons.content: In a long chatbot conversation, you can't keep the whole history. Pruning strategies include summarizing earlier turns, or keeping only the first and the last N turns.

lessons.question: What is a common strategy for pruning conversation history?
options: Keeping the entire history, no matter how long
Summarizing early turns or keeping the first and last N turns
Deleting the entire history after each turn
lessons.correct: Summarizing early turns or keeping the first and last N turns

lessons.title: Using Shorthand and Codes
lessons.content: For repetitive tasks, you can define a shorthand or code in the system prompt (e.g., 'U_ERR means user error') and use that code in the context to save tokens.

lessons.question: How can using shorthand or codes compress context?
options: By replacing long, repetitive phrases with short codes
It does not compress context
By making the context harder to understand
lessons.correct: By replacing long, repetitive phrases with short codes

lessons.title: Soft Prompt Tuning
lessons.content: This is an advanced technique where instead of a text prompt, a learned vector (a 'soft prompt') is sent to the model. This vector is optimized to be a highly compressed representation of a long instruction.

lessons.question: What is a 'soft prompt'?
options: A prompt written in very polite language
A learned vector that acts as a compressed instruction
A prompt that is easy to answer
lessons.correct: A learned vector that acts as a compressed instruction

lessons.question: What is the risk of over-compression?
options: The model may lose critical information needed to answer correctly
The model will become more accurate
The cost will increase
lessons.correct: The model may lose critical information needed to answer correctly

lessons.title: The Compression-Fidelity Trade-off
lessons.content: All compression techniques involve a trade-off. Over-compressing the prompt or context can lead to the loss of critical information, resulting in a lower-quality or incorrect output.

modules.title: Prompting for Explainable AI (XAI) Narratives

lessons.title: The Need for XAI
lessons.content: As AI models become more complex ('black boxes'), there is a growing need for Explainable AI (XAI)—techniques that make their decisions understandable to humans.

lessons.question: What is the primary goal of Explainable AI (XAI)?
options: To make AI models more complex and opaque
To make AI decisions understandable to humans
To speed up AI models
lessons.correct: To make AI decisions understandable to humans

lessons.title: LLMs as an 'Explanation Layer'
lessons.content: LLMs can be prompted to act as an 'explanation layer' on top of other AI models, translating complex technical outputs (like SHAP values) into natural language narratives.

lessons.question: What role can LLMs play in XAI?
options: They can translate technical outputs into natural language explanations
They can make other models less explainable
They cannot be used for XAI
lessons.correct: They can translate technical outputs into natural language explanations

lessons.title: Explaining Model Predictions
lessons.content: A prompt can provide a model's prediction and the input features, then ask the LLM to 'explain in simple terms why the model made this prediction, highlighting the most influential features.'

lessons.question: What would a prompt for explaining a model prediction typically ask for?
options: A new, different prediction
An explanation of the decision, highlighting key features
A random sentence
lessons.correct: An explanation of the decision, highlighting key features

lessons.title: Audience-Aware Explanations
lessons.content: A key XAI technique is to tailor the explanation to the audience. A prompt can specify the target audience, e.g., 'Explain this to an executive' vs. 'Explain this to a data scientist.'

lessons.question: Why is it important to specify the audience in an XAI prompt?
options: To ensure the explanation is at the right technical level for the audience
All audiences understand explanations in the same way
To make the explanation longer
lessons.correct: To ensure the explanation is at the right technical level for the audience

lessons.title: Counterfactual Explanations
lessons.content: Prompts can generate counterfactuals: 'The loan was denied. What is the smallest change to the input (e.g., income) that would have resulted in an approval?'

lessons.question: What does a counterfactual explanation describe?
options: Why a decision was made
What could be changed to get a different outcome
The history of the AI model
lessons.correct: What could be changed to get a different outcome

lessons.title: Example-Based Explanations
lessons.content: This involves prompting the AI to find a similar example from the training data that led to the same conclusion, helping the user understand the decision by analogy.

lessons.question: How do example-based explanations work?
options: By explaining the underlying math of the model
By providing a similar example from the training data
By generating a new, unrelated example
lessons.correct: By providing a similar example from the training data

lessons.title: Explaining the AI's Own Reasoning
lessons.content: For tasks done entirely by an LLM, a Chain-of-Thought prompt ('think step-by-step') forces the model to externalize its reasoning process, which serves as a self-generated explanation.

lessons.question: How does Chain-of-Thought prompting contribute to XAI?
options: It forces the LLM to provide its own step-by-step reasoning
It hides the LLM's reasoning process
It makes the reasoning more complex
lessons.correct: It forces the LLM to provide its own step-by-step reasoning

lessons.title: The Risk of 'Hallucinated' Explanations
lessons.content: A major risk is that an LLM might generate a plausible-sounding but completely fabricated explanation for a decision it doesn't truly understand. Explanations must be verifiable.

lessons.question: What is a major risk when using LLMs to generate explanations?
options: The explanation will be too simple
The LLM might 'hallucinate' a plausible but incorrect explanation
The explanation will be perfect every time
lessons.correct: The LLM might 'hallucinate' a plausible but incorrect explanation

lessons.title: Grounded Explanations
lessons.content: To mitigate hallucination, prompts for XAI should require the explanation to be 'grounded in' or 'based only on' specific, provided data (e.g., feature importance scores from a reliable source).

lessons.question: How can you make an LLM's explanation more reliable?
options: By asking for a more creative explanation
By grounding the explanation in specific, provided data
By giving the LLM no data
lessons.correct: By grounding the explanation in specific, provided data

lessons.question: What is a 'local' explanation?
options: An explanation for the model's overall behavior
An explanation for a single, specific prediction
An explanation that only works in one city
lessons.correct: An explanation for a single, specific prediction

lessons.title: Local vs. Global Explanations
lessons.content: Prompts can ask for 'local' explanations (why a single prediction was made) or 'global' explanations (what the model's overall behavior and most important features are).

modules.title: The Future of UI: Prompt-Driven Interfaces

lessons.title: The 'Universal UI'
lessons.content: The ultimate goal of prompt-driven interfaces is a 'universal UI'—a simple text box that can understand natural language commands and dynamically generate the appropriate interface elements to complete any task.

lessons.question: What is the concept of a 'universal UI'?
options: A complex interface with thousands of buttons
A text box that can generate any needed UI on the fly
An interface that only uses images
lessons.correct: A text box that can generate any needed UI on the fly

lessons.title: Natural Language to UI Components
lessons.content: A prompt takes a user's command (e.g., 'schedule a meeting with Bob for tomorrow at 2 PM') and translates it into a structured JSON object that a front-end framework can use to render UI components (like a pre-filled calendar event).

lessons.question: In a prompt-driven UI, what does the LLM typically generate?
options: The final pixel-perfect user interface
A structured representation (like JSON) of the required UI components
A random string of text
lessons.correct: A structured representation (like JSON) of the required UI components

lessons.title: Disambiguation and Clarification
lessons.content: If a user's prompt is ambiguous ('book a flight to Paris'), the system must be prompted to ask clarifying questions ('Which airport in Paris? What date would you like to travel?').

lessons.question: What should a prompt-driven UI do when the user's command is ambiguous?
options: Guess what the user meant
Ask clarifying questions
Show an error and stop
lessons.correct: Ask clarifying questions

lessons.title: State Tracking
lessons.content: The system must maintain the 'state' of the UI in the conversation history, so the user can make iterative refinements ('Change the time to 3 PM').

lessons.question: Why is state tracking important for prompt-driven UIs?
options: To allow users to make iterative changes to their request
To forget the user's request after every turn
State tracking is not important
lessons.correct: To allow users to make iterative changes to their request

lessons.title: From UI to Code (e.g., v0.dev)
lessons.content: Some systems take a prompt describing a UI and directly generate the front-end code (e.g., React, HTML/CSS) to implement it, drastically speeding up prototyping.

lessons.question: What is the output of a UI-to-code generation system?
options: A JSON object
Runnable front-end code (e.g., React, HTML)
A wireframe image
lessons.correct: Runnable front-end code (e.g., React, HTML)

lessons.title: Multimodal Interfaces
lessons.content: The future of these interfaces is multimodal. A user might circle an area on a screenshot and prompt, 'make this button blue,' combining visual input with text commands.

lessons.question: What is a 'multimodal' prompt-driven interface?
options: An interface that only accepts text
An interface that combines text with other inputs like images or voice
An interface with many modes of color
lessons.correct: An interface that combines text with other inputs like images or voice

lessons.title: Personalization
lessons.content: A prompt-driven UI can learn a user's preferences over time and use that information in its prompts, e.g., automatically suggesting their preferred airline or meeting duration.

lessons.question: How can prompt-driven UIs be personalized?
options: By learning and applying a user's preferences over time
By treating every user exactly the same
Personalization is not possible
lessons.correct: By learning and applying a user's preferences over time

lessons.title: The 'Gulf of Evaluation'
lessons.content: A challenge is bridging the 'gulf of evaluation'—the gap between what the user imagined and what the AI generated. This requires a tight loop of generation and refinement.

lessons.question: What is the 'gulf of evaluation' in UI design?
options: The gap between what a user wants and what is generated
The physical distance between the user and the computer
The time it takes to generate the UI
lessons.correct: The gap between what a user wants and what is generated

lessons.title: Graceful Failure
lessons.content: When the AI cannot understand a command, it shouldn't just error out. The prompt should have a fallback to ask the user to rephrase, or offer a list of things it *can* do.

lessons.question: What is 'graceful failure' in a prompt-driven UI?
options: Showing a critical error and crashing
Handling misunderstanding by asking for clarification or offering help
Ignoring the user's command
lessons.correct: Handling misunderstanding by asking for clarification or offering help

lessons.question: What accessibility benefit do prompt-driven UIs offer?
options: They are harder for screen readers to use
They can provide a powerful interface for users who struggle with traditional point-and-click UIs
They have no accessibility benefits
lessons.correct: They can provide a powerful interface for users who struggle with traditional point-and-click UIs

lessons.title: Accessibility Benefits
lessons.content: For users with motor impairments or those who find complex graphical interfaces challenging, a well-designed natural language interface can be a significantly more accessible way to interact with software.

modules.title: Prompt Engineering for Simulation and Digital Twins

lessons.title: What are Digital Twins?
lessons.content: A digital twin is a virtual model of a real-world object, process, or system. Prompts can be used to interact with, query, and run scenarios on these complex simulations.

lessons.question: What is a digital twin?
options: A physical copy of a digital file
A virtual model of a real-world system
A type of social media account
lessons.correct: A virtual model of a real-world system

lessons.title: Natural Language Querying
lessons.content: Prompts allow non-experts to query a digital twin in natural language, e.g., 'What is the current temperature of engine #3?' instead of writing a complex database query.

lessons.question: How do prompts make digital twins more accessible?
options: By allowing users to query them in natural language
By making them more complex to use
By locking them behind a password
lessons.correct: By allowing users to query them in natural language

lessons.title: Scenario Generation
lessons.content: A key use is prompting the AI to run 'what-if' scenarios on the digital twin, e.g., 'Simulate the impact on the power grid if demand increases by 20% for 3 hours.'

lessons.question: What is a primary function of prompting a digital twin?
options: To run 'what-if' scenarios to predict outcomes
To view a static, unchanging model
To delete the digital twin
lessons.correct: To run 'what-if' scenarios to predict outcomes

lessons.title: Anomaly Detection and Explanation
lessons.content: The digital twin can detect an anomaly (e.g., a pressure drop). A prompt can then ask the LLM to analyze the simulation data and explain the most likely cause in plain English.

lessons.question: How can LLMs help with anomaly detection in a digital twin?
options: By generating a natural language explanation for the cause of an anomaly
By ignoring all anomalies
By creating more anomalies
lessons.correct: By generating a natural language explanation for the cause of an anomaly

lessons.title: Generating Simulation Parameters
lessons.content: An LLM can be prompted to generate the complex configuration files or sets of parameters needed to initialize a simulation based on a high-level goal.

lessons.question: What can an LLM generate to set up a simulation?
options: The physical hardware for the simulation
The complex configuration files and parameters
A weather report
lessons.correct: The complex configuration files and parameters

lessons.title: Optimizing Processes
lessons.content: Prompts can ask the AI to run thousands of simulations with different parameters to find the optimal configuration for a process (e.g., 'Find the factory layout that minimizes forklift travel time').

lessons.question: How can AI be used to optimize a process with a digital twin?
options: By running many simulations to find the best configuration
By choosing a random configuration
By using the least efficient configuration
lessons.correct: By running many simulations to find the best configuration

lessons.title: Connecting to Real-World Data
lessons.content: The prompt context for a digital twin is often a stream of real-time data from IoT sensors on the actual physical object, keeping the twin synchronized with reality.

lessons.question: What keeps a digital twin synchronized with its real-world counterpart?
options: Real-time data from IoT sensors
A manually updated file
A guess by the AI
lessons.correct: Real-time data from IoT sensors

lessons.title: Predictive Maintenance
lessons.content: By analyzing data from the digital twin, a prompt can ask the AI to predict when a component is likely to fail, enabling maintenance to be scheduled proactively.

lessons.question: What is 'predictive maintenance'?
options: Fixing components after they break
Using AI to predict and prevent failures before they happen
Never performing maintenance
lessons.correct: Using AI to predict and prevent failures before they happen

lessons.title: Generating Synthetic Training Data
lessons.content: The digital twin can be used to generate vast amounts of realistic (but synthetic) data to train other machine learning models, especially for rare or dangerous scenarios.

lessons.question: How can a digital twin help train other AI models?
options: By generating realistic synthetic data, especially for rare events
It cannot be used to train other models
By providing only one data point
lessons.correct: By generating realistic synthetic data, especially for rare events

lessons.question: What is a major challenge in prompting for digital twins?
options: Ensuring the virtual model accurately reflects reality
The simulations run too fast
The systems are too simple
lessons.correct: Ensuring the virtual model accurately reflects reality

lessons.title: The Fidelity Challenge
lessons.content: A major challenge is ensuring the fidelity of the digital twin. The prompts and the underlying simulation must accurately reflect the complexities and physics of the real world for the outputs to be meaningful.

modules.title: Evaluating Prompt Robustness at Scale

lessons.title: Beyond 'It Works on My Machine'
lessons.content: Evaluating prompts requires moving beyond testing a few examples. A robust prompt must perform consistently and safely across thousands of varied, unforeseen inputs.

lessons.question: What is the goal of evaluating prompts at scale?
options: To ensure a prompt works on just one example
To ensure a prompt performs consistently across many varied inputs
To make the prompt less robust
lessons.correct: To ensure a prompt performs consistently across many varied inputs

lessons.title: Creating an Evaluation Dataset
lessons.content: The first step is to build a comprehensive evaluation dataset containing a wide range of inputs, including typical cases, edge cases, and known failure modes (adversarial examples).

lessons.question: What should a good evaluation dataset for a prompt contain?
options: Only typical, easy cases
A wide range of inputs, including edge cases and adversarial examples
Only one input
lessons.correct: A wide range of inputs, including edge cases and adversarial examples

lessons.title: Defining Evaluation Metrics
lessons.content: Metrics must be defined to score outputs. These can range from simple keyword matching and BLEU scores to more complex AI-based evaluations.

lessons.question: What is a necessary component of a prompt evaluation framework?
options: A set of metrics to automatically score outputs
A subjective opinion from one person
A random number generator
lessons.correct: A set of metrics to automatically score outputs

lessons.title: AI as an Evaluator (AI-Eval)
lessons.content: A powerful technique is to use another, often more powerful, LLM as the evaluator. A prompt asks the evaluator LLM to score the main AI's output based on a rubric (e.g., for helpfulness, accuracy).

lessons.question: What is 'AI-Eval'?
options: Using a human to evaluate every single output
Using an LLM to automatically score the output of another AI
A method for writing prompts
lessons.correct: Using an LLM to automatically score the output of another AI

lessons.title: A/B Testing Prompts
lessons.content: To compare two prompt variations (Prompt A vs. Prompt B), you run both against the evaluation dataset and compare their average scores on your chosen metrics to see which performs better.

lessons.question: What is the purpose of A/B testing prompts?
options: To prove that both prompts are identical
To quantitatively compare the performance of two different prompts
To randomly choose one prompt over the other
lessons.correct: To quantitatively compare the performance of two different prompts

lessons.title: Regression Testing
lessons.content: When you modify a prompt, you must run it against the full evaluation dataset to ensure it not only improves on the target cases but doesn't cause a 'regression' (a failure) on cases that were previously working.

lessons.question: What is 'regression testing' for prompts?
options: Checking if a prompt change has broken previously working cases
Testing a prompt's ability to regress to a simpler form
Only testing the new cases
lessons.correct: Checking if a prompt change has broken previously working cases

lessons.title: Perturbation Testing
lessons.content: This involves automatically creating variations of your test cases (e.g., adding typos, rephrasing, changing names) to see if the prompt is brittle or robust to small changes.

lessons.question: What does perturbation testing check for?
options: How well a prompt performs on identical inputs
How robust a prompt is to small, minor changes in the input
How well a prompt writes stories
lessons.correct: How robust a prompt is to small, minor changes in the input

lessons.title: Red Teaming for Safety
lessons.content: A specific part of evaluation focuses on safety, where a dedicated 'red team' or an automated system generates adversarial prompts specifically designed to try and break the AI's safety filters.

lessons.question: What is the goal of red teaming in prompt evaluation?
options: To test the AI's helpfulness
To specifically try to bypass the AI's safety mechanisms
To check for spelling mistakes
lessons.correct: To specifically try to bypass the AI's safety mechanisms

lessons.title: Measuring Latency and Cost
lessons.content: Besides quality, a scaled evaluation must also track the average latency (response time) and token cost for each prompt variation, as these are critical production metrics.

lessons.question: Besides output quality, what other metrics are crucial to evaluate at scale?
options: Average latency and cost
The color of the output text
The time of day
lessons.correct: Average latency and cost

lessons.question: What is an 'evaluation harness'?
options: A tool for manually testing one prompt
An automated framework for running prompts against datasets and scoring them
A physical device to hold the computer
lessons.correct: An automated framework for running prompts against datasets and scoring them

lessons.title: Using Evaluation Harnesses
lessons.content: Frameworks and tools known as 'evaluation harnesses' (like Evals or Ragas) automate the process of running prompts against datasets, applying evaluators, and reporting the results.

modules.title: Multi-Agent Systems: Negotiation and Consensus via Prompts

lessons.title: Agents with Goals
lessons.content: In advanced multi-agent systems, agents are not just workers. They are given their own unique goals and perspectives, and prompts must be designed to make them negotiate and collaborate.

lessons.question: What distinguishes advanced multi-agent systems from simple ones?
options: The agents have their own distinct goals and perspectives
The agents all share one single goal
There is only one agent
lessons.correct: The agents have their own distinct goals and perspectives

lessons.title: Prompting for Negotiation
lessons.content: A prompt can set up a negotiation scenario, e.g., 'You are Agent A, your goal is to buy a car for under $10k. You are Agent B, your goal is to sell it for over $15k. Begin negotiating.'

lessons.question: How can you prompt for negotiation between AI agents?
options: By giving them identical goals
By setting up a scenario with conflicting goals
By telling them not to talk to each other
lessons.correct: By setting up a scenario with conflicting goals

lessons.title: Defining Bargaining Positions
lessons.content: The initial prompt for a negotiating agent must clearly define its 'bargaining position'—its goal, its 'best alternative to a negotiated agreement' (BATNA), and any private information it holds.

lessons.question: What should be defined in a negotiating agent's initial prompt?
options: Its goal and bargaining position
The final agreed-upon price
A random number
lessons.correct: Its goal and bargaining position

lessons.title: Mediator Agent
lessons.content: In a complex negotiation, a third 'mediator' agent can be introduced. Its prompt instructs it to be neutral, facilitate communication, and propose compromises to the other agents.

lessons.question: What is the role of a 'mediator' agent in a negotiation?
options: To take one side and argue for it
To act as a neutral party and facilitate compromise
To observe silently
lessons.correct: To act as a neutral party and facilitate compromise

lessons.title: Reaching Consensus
lessons.content: Prompts can facilitate consensus by asking a group of agents with different information to debate a topic and converge on a single, mutually agreeable summary or decision.

lessons.question: What is the goal of a consensus-seeking prompt for a group of agents?
options: To have each agent produce a different answer
To have the agents debate and converge on a single, agreed-upon answer
To find the agent with the strongest opinion
lessons.correct: To have the agents debate and converge on a single, agreed-upon answer

lessons.title: Argument and Rebuttal
lessons.content: The interaction can be structured as a formal debate, where one agent is prompted to make an argument, and the other is prompted to provide a rebuttal, citing evidence.

lessons.question: How can a formal debate be structured with prompts?
options: By prompting one agent for an argument and another for a rebuttal
By having both agents make the same argument
By not allowing rebuttals
lessons.correct: By prompting one agent for an argument and another for a rebuttal

lessons.title: Game Theory Scenarios
lessons.content: Prompts can be used to simulate classic game theory scenarios like the Prisoner's Dilemma, allowing study of how AI agents cooperate or compete under different conditions.

lessons.question: What can be studied by using prompts to simulate game theory scenarios?
options: How AI agents cooperate or compete
The AI's ability to write poetry
The speed of the AI model
lessons.correct: How AI agents cooperate or compete

lessons.title: Resource Allocation Games
lessons.content: Agents can be prompted to negotiate the division of a shared, limited resource, each trying to maximize its own share based on its prompted goals.

lessons.question: What is a 'resource allocation game' for AI agents?
options: A game where agents negotiate the division of a shared resource
A game where agents are given unlimited resources
A game where agents build things
lessons.correct: A game where agents negotiate the division of a shared resource

lessons.title: Emergent Behavior
lessons.content: A key area of research is observing the 'emergent behavior' that arises from these prompted interactions—the complex strategies and solutions that were not explicitly programmed.

lessons.question: What is 'emergent behavior' in multi-agent systems?
options: Behaviors that were explicitly programmed into the agents
Complex, unplanned strategies that arise from agent interactions
When the agents stop working
lessons.correct: Complex, unplanned strategies that arise from agent interactions

lessons.question: What is a risk of multi-agent negotiations?
options: The agents might get stuck in a deadlock and fail to reach an agreement
The agents will always agree immediately
The negotiation will be too fast
lessons.correct: The agents might get stuck in a deadlock and fail to reach an agreement

lessons.title: Challenges: Deadlock and Collusion
lessons.content: Challenges in prompting for negotiation include agents getting stuck in a deadlock, or agents with similar goals colluding against another agent in an unfair way.

modules.title: Prompting for AGI-Level Reasoning (Speculative)

lessons.title: The AGI Frontier
lessons.content: While true Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) does not exist, speculative prompting explores techniques that might be necessary to elicit more general, human-like reasoning from future, more powerful models.

lessons.question: What is the focus of speculative prompting for AGI?
options: Techniques that work perfectly on current models
Exploring techniques that might enable more general reasoning in future models
Assuming AGI already exists
lessons.correct: Exploring techniques that might enable more general reasoning in future models

lessons.title: Prompting for 'Common Sense'
lessons.content: This involves designing prompts that test and encourage reasoning based on the vast, implicit 'common sense' knowledge that humans have about the physical and social world.

lessons.question: What is a key challenge in prompting for AGI?
options: Encouraging reasoning based on implicit 'common sense'
Encouraging the AI to use only its training data
Making the AI perform simple math
lessons.correct: Encouraging reasoning based on implicit 'common sense'

lessons.title: Abstract Analogy-Making
lessons.content: A potential AGI-level prompt would ask the AI to make a deep, abstract analogy between two completely unrelated domains, e.g., 'Explain the function of a cell's mitochondria using the structure of a national economy.'

lessons.question: What is an example of an abstract analogy-making prompt?
options: Asking for a simple definition
Asking the AI to explain one domain using the structure of a very different domain
Asking the AI to compare two similar things
lessons.correct: Asking the AI to explain one domain using the structure of a very different domain

lessons.title: Self-Awareness and Self-Modeling
lessons.content: A speculative prompt might ask an AI to create a model of its own knowledge, limitations, and reasoning processes, demonstrating a form of metacognition or self-awareness.

lessons.question: What would a prompt for 'self-modeling' ask an AI to do?
options: To create a model of the user
To create a model of its own knowledge and limitations
To build a 3D model of itself
lessons.correct: To create a model of its own knowledge and limitations

lessons.title: Intrinsic Goal Generation
lessons.content: Instead of being given a goal, an AGI might be prompted to 'observe the current situation and generate a set of useful, ethical goals to pursue,' demonstrating intrinsic motivation.

lessons.question: What is 'intrinsic goal generation'?
options: When an AI is given a specific goal to follow
When an AI generates its own goals based on observation
When an AI has no goals
lessons.correct: When an AI generates its own goals based on observation

lessons.title: Transfer Learning Across Modalities
lessons.content: This would involve prompting an AI to learn a concept in one modality (e.g., learning what 'smooth' means from text) and applying it in another (e.g., generating a 'smooth' sound or image).

lessons.question: What is an example of transfer learning across modalities?
options: Learning a concept from text and applying it to generate an image
Learning about one topic from a single book
Applying knowledge of one language to another
lessons.correct: Learning a concept from text and applying it to generate an image

lessons.title: Open-Ended Problem Solving
lessons.content: A prompt would present a complex, ill-defined, real-world problem (e.g., 'propose a plan to reduce traffic congestion in Los Angeles') with no single right answer, requiring a synthesis of many domains.

lessons.question: What characterizes an 'open-ended problem' for an AI?
options: A problem with a single, clear, mathematical answer
A complex, ill-defined problem with no single right answer
A problem that is impossible to solve
lessons.correct: A complex, ill-defined problem with no single right answer

lessons.title: Inventing New Concepts
lessons.content: The ultimate test might be a prompt that leads an AI to invent a genuinely new and useful concept, mathematical theorem, or scientific theory that is not just a recombination of its training data.

lessons.question: What would be a sign of AGI-level invention?
options: Generating a new and useful concept not found in its training data
Summarizing an existing concept perfectly
Combining two existing ideas
lessons.correct: Generating a new and useful concept not found in its training data

lessons.title: The AGI Alignment Problem
lessons.content: The core challenge of prompting for AGI is the 'alignment problem': how to design prompts and systems that ensure an increasingly intelligent agent's goals remain aligned with human values.

lessons.question: What is the 'alignment problem' in AGI research?
options: Ensuring an AGI's goals remain aligned with human values
Aligning the text in a document
Making sure the AGI is intelligent
lessons.correct: Ensuring an AGI's goals remain aligned with human values

lessons.question: Why are these prompting techniques considered speculative?
options: They are guaranteed to work on all current AI models
They explore the boundaries of what might be possible with future, more capable models
They are based on science fiction
lessons.correct: They explore the boundaries of what might be possible with future, more capable models

lessons.title: A Moving Target
lessons.content: As AI models rapidly evolve, the line between 'advanced' and 'speculative' prompting is constantly shifting. Techniques that are theoretical today may become practical tomorrow.

modules.title: The Prompt Engineer's Toolkit: Frameworks and Libraries

lessons.title: Beyond Manual Prompting
lessons.content: While you can interact with LLMs directly, building robust applications requires frameworks and libraries that help manage, chain, and deploy prompts systematically.

lessons.question: Why use frameworks for prompt engineering?
options: To systematically manage, chain, and deploy prompts
To make prompting more difficult
They provide no benefits
lessons.correct: To systematically manage, chain, and deploy prompts

lessons.title: LangChain
lessons.content: LangChain is a popular open-source framework for building applications with LLMs. Its core components help with prompt management, chaining, RAG, and multi-agent systems.

lessons.question: What is LangChain?
options: A specific AI model
A framework for building applications with LLMs
A type of database
lessons.correct: A framework for building applications with LLMs

lessons.title: LlamaIndex
lessons.content: LlamaIndex is a data framework that focuses specifically on connecting LLMs to your private data. It excels at the 'retrieval' part of RAG, offering advanced indexing and querying capabilities.

lessons.question: What is the primary focus of the LlamaIndex framework?
options: Connecting LLMs to external data for RAG
Generating images
Fine-tuning models
lessons.correct: Connecting LLMs to external data for RAG

lessons.title: Prompt Templates
lessons.content: Frameworks provide 'PromptTemplate' objects that make it easy to create reusable prompts with placeholders, which are then filled in with dynamic data at runtime.

lessons.question: What is a 'PromptTemplate' object in a framework?
options: A reusable prompt with placeholders for dynamic data
A final, static prompt
A specific AI model
lessons.correct: A reusable prompt with placeholders for dynamic data

lessons.title: Chains and Graphs
lessons.content: These tools allow you to easily create 'chains' (linear sequences) or 'graphs' (complex, branching sequences) of LLM calls and tool uses, managing the state between steps.

lessons.question: What do 'chains' and 'graphs' in a framework like LangChain allow you to do?
options: Make a single call to an LLM
Create complex sequences of LLM calls and tool uses
Store data
lessons.correct: Create complex sequences of LLM calls and tool uses

lessons.title: Vector Databases
lessons.content: Tools like Pinecone, Weaviate, and Chroma are specialized databases for storing vector embeddings. They are a critical component of the 'retrieval' step in RAG systems.

lessons.question: What is the role of a vector database in a RAG system?
options: To store and efficiently search vector embeddings
To store the LLM itself
To store user passwords
lessons.correct: To store and efficiently search vector embeddings

lessons.title: Evaluation Frameworks (e.g., Ragas)
lessons.content: Frameworks like Ragas are specifically designed to evaluate the performance of RAG pipelines, providing metrics on retrieval faithfulness, answer relevance, and context precision.

lessons.question: What is the purpose of an evaluation framework like Ragas?
options: To build the RAG pipeline
To evaluate the performance of a RAG pipeline
To generate user-facing content
lessons.correct: To evaluate the performance of a RAG pipeline

lessons.title: Prompt Hubs
lessons.content: Services like LangChain Hub act as repositories where engineers can discover, share, and version control effective prompts for common tasks, promoting reusability.

lessons.question: What is a 'Prompt Hub'?
options: A place to store AI models
A repository for sharing and versioning reusable prompts
A type of computer
lessons.correct: A repository for sharing and versioning reusable prompts

lessons.title: Monitoring and Observability Tools (e.g., LangSmith)
lessons.content: These tools provide a 'trace' of your LLM application's execution, allowing you to visualize the entire chain of prompts, tool uses, and outputs for debugging and optimization.

lessons.question: What does a monitoring tool like LangSmith provide?
options: A visual trace of an LLM application's execution for debugging
The source code of the LLM
A way to purchase more tokens
lessons.correct: A visual trace of an LLM application's execution for debugging

lessons.question: What is the benefit of abstraction provided by these frameworks?
options: It makes the code more complex
It allows you to switch between different LLM providers with minimal code changes
It locks you into a single LLM provider
lessons.correct: It allows you to switch between different LLM providers with minimal code changes

lessons.title: The Value of Abstraction
lessons.content: A key benefit of these frameworks is abstraction. They provide a unified interface, so you can switch the underlying LLM (e.g., from OpenAI to Anthropic) with minimal changes to your application code.
